 These ﬁndings suggest that individuals may require different amounts of die-
tary LA, ALA, or AA, EPA, and DHA, for both normal development and in the prevention and management of chronic diseases.
The interaction between dietary factors and genetic variants could explain the differences noted in association studies. Consid-
ering that a low omega-3 intake in the presence of certain genetic variants leads to a more aggressive disease, an increase in omega-3
intake and a decrease in omega-6 leading to a balanced omega-6/omega-3 ratio may be a sensible recommendation to reduce
disease risk in the general population. Nutrigenetics/nutrigenomics will continue to provide data on mechanisms of nutrients
and gene interactions in both health and disease.
